candidate_sources.title: Weir's Cushion Rust of Spruces - Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Do not accept and plant landscape or nursery stock affected by Weir's cushion rust. Inspect established spruce trees in late summer and fall for evidence (yellow spots and bands on current year's needles). Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil; make the first application when 10% of buds have broken and two additional applications at seven to 10 day intervals. Colorado blue spruce is particularly susceptible.

candidate_sources.title: Weir's Cushion Rust of Spruce : Landscape : Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment (CAFE) at UMass Amherst
candidate_sources.snippet: Weir's cushion rust, caused by Chrysomyxa weirii, is unusual among rust diseases in that it does not need an alternate host and survives solely on spruce. In late winter to early spring, orange to yellow spots or bands appear on one-year-old needles; bands swell to produce waxy, yellow-orange pustules containing masses of rust-colored spores. C. weirii is monocyclic.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Weir's Cushion Rust on Colorado Blue Spruce Caused by Chrysomyxa weirii in Michigan | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Trees affected by this disease initially exhibit nondiagnostic yellowish-orange spots and chlorotic bands with blister-like pustules developing throughout the summer on current-year needles. Confirms Chrysomyxa weirii on Colorado blue spruce (Picea pungens) as the causal agent of Weir's cushion rust.

candidate_sources.title: Bands from Weir's cushion rust visible on infected spruce needles - MSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Weir's cushion rust is first noticeable as yellow flecks on needles in winter. As bud break approaches in early to mid-May, the bands swell to produce waxy, yellow-orange pustules. It is mostly a cosmetic problem but in some cases can cause severe premature defoliation of spruce.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizosphaera Needle Cast Disease of Blue Spruce | New Mexico State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizosphaera needle cast is a fungus disease caused by Rhizosphaera kalkhoffii, primarily affecting blue spruce (Picea pungens). Infected needles turn yellow then reddish-purple before turning brown and falling off. The fungus can be seen with a hand lens as tiny brown to black pycnidia (fruiting bodies) emerging from stomata on the needles.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizosphaera needle cast | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: The first noticeable symptom is purpling or browning and loss of the innermost needles on lower branches, while the youngest needles at the tips often remain healthy. Tiny black bumps (pycnidia) arranged in neat rows appear on infected needles. Management includes avoiding overhead irrigation, removing dead needles, and fungicide applications of chlorothalonil, copper hydroxide or mancozeb.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizosphaera Needle Cast | Yard and Garden â€” Iowa State University Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Infected needles turn yellow in July and then reddish-purple in August before turning brown and falling off. Infection takes place in the spring but symptoms are not visible until the following spring and summer. The disease starts on lower branches and gradually moves up the tree year after year. Apply fungicide when new needles are half mature length, with a second application 3 to 4 weeks later.

candidate_sources.title: Spruce (Picea spp.)-Rhizosphaera Needle Cast | Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks
candidate_sources.snippet: Rhizosphaera needle cast of spruce caused by Rhizosphaera kalkhoffii. Details symptoms, disease cycle and chemical/cultural management for spruce species including Colorado blue spruce.

candidate_sources.title: Spruce needle rust | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Spruce needle rust is caused by fungi from several species of the genus Chrysomyxa. Young needles on infected trees turn yellow, and severely infected trees have a tan to pinkish look. Colorado blue, white and black spruce are most commonly affected. Needle rust is not a significant threat to the health of the tree.

candidate_sources.title: Spruce Needle Rusts in Connecticut | Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station
candidate_sources.snippet: Spruce needle rusts are caused by several species of Chrysomyxa, including C. ledi, C. ledicola, and C. weirii. Some are heteroecious requiring alternate hosts such as Labrador tea and leatherleaf, while Chrysomyxa weirii is autoecious. Symptoms include yellow spotting and banding on needles with yellow-orange pustules.

candidate_sources.title: Spruce Needle Rust | UMass Center for Agriculture, Food, and the Environment
candidate_sources.snippet: Spruce needle rust, caused by fungi in the genus Chrysomyxa, produces orange to yellow spots or bands on one-year-old needles that swell into waxy yellow-orange pustules containing rust-colored spores. Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, beginning when 10% of buds have broken.
